guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer: Stories get turned away when they are too short or too long, when a sentence runs past twenty words, when they use words the tiny mind has not met much before, or when they change the character’s name, kind, or two special things. If a story only has a few unknown words wrong, the ghostwriter gets one automatic repair; these are fixed checks, not a judgment of quality.
problems: Says words the model 'has not met much before'; the rule is words it met in the stories it grew up on.
Adds 'kind' as a required fact, but the visible editor shows only name and two facts; this may be unsupported from the current screen.
Includes extra detail about an automatic repair by the ghostwriter, which is not asked for and not grounded in the shown status.

guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer: Stories can get turned away because they must be between one hundred and one hundred eighty words long, have no sentences longer than twenty words, use words the tiny mind has learned from its stories, and keep the character's facts word for word. If a story only has a few unknown words, it can get fixed automatically. These are fixed rules, not a judgment of quality. Do: SHOW writer.

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer: Attention can hint at which parts matter, but it is only a clue, not proof. Switching parts off tests whether the fact actually breaks, so it gives causal evidence instead of just a pattern.

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer:
Switching parts off helps measure causal contributions to the prediction, showing how much each part really matters. Attention can suggest connections but doesn't reveal if those parts are essential. With ablation, we can find out which components truly affect the outcome.
